claim: Sensory receptive fields are large enough that they can contain more than one perceptible stimulus.
source: Sensory receptive fields are large enough that they can contain more than one perceptible stimulus.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory receptive fields that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: When more than one stimulus is present, single neurons can fluctuate between coding one vs. the other(s) across some time period.
source: We recently showed that when more than one stimulus is present, single neurons can fluctuate between coding one vs. the other(s) across some time period, suggesting a form of neural multiplexing of different stimuli (Caruso et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Coding fluctuations occur in macaque V1 but only when the two stimuli form separate objects.
source: We found coding fluctuations do occur in macaque V1 but only when the two stimuli form separate objects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Separate objects evoked a novel pattern of V1 spike count ('noise') correlations involving distinct distributions of positive and negative values.
source: Such separate objects evoked a novel pattern of V1 spike count ('noise') correlations involving distinct distributions of positive and negative values.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bimodal correlation pattern was most pronounced among pairs of neurons showing the strongest evidence for coding fluctuations or multiplexing.
source: This bimodal correlation pattern was most pronounced among pairs of neurons showing the strongest evidence for coding fluctuations or multiplexing.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Whether a given pair of neurons exhibited positive or negative correlations depended on whether the two neurons both responded better to the same object or had different object preferences.
source: Whether a given pair of neurons exhibited positive or negative correlations depended on whether the two neurons both responded better to the same object or had different object preferences.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Pairs of neurons with the same object preference showed median correlation of +0.25.
source: Whether the correlations tended to be positive vs. negative depended on whether the two neurons in the pair preferred the same stimulus (median correlation + 0.25) or preferred different stimuli (median correlation –0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Pairs of neurons with different object preferences showed median correlation of -0.05.
source: Whether the correlations tended to be positive vs. negative depended on whether the two neurons in the pair preferred the same stimulus (median correlation + 0.25) or preferred different stimuli (median correlation –0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Among pairs of neurons showing fluctuating activity, those with same preference showed median correlation of +0.49.
source: The distribution of spike count correlation values was even more widely spread among pairs of neurons that showed demonstrably fluctuating activity across stimulus presentations (same preference: +0.49 and different preference: –0.14).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Among pairs of neurons showing fluctuating activity, those with different preference showed median correlation of -0.14.
source: The distribution of spike count correlation values was even more widely spread among pairs of neurons that showed demonstrably fluctuating activity across stimulus presentations (same preference: +0.49 and different preference: –0.14).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: For single stimuli, the median spike count correlation was 0.15-0.19.
source: In contrast, in the single stimuli and fused object (superimposed gratings) cases, positive correlations predominated (single stimuli: median value 0.15–0.19; fused object: median value +0.15).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: For fused objects (superimposed gratings), the median spike count correlation was +0.15.
source: In contrast, in the single stimuli and fused object (superimposed gratings) cases, positive correlations predominated (single stimuli: median value 0.15–0.19; fused object: median value +0.15).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Distinct tuning-preference-related distributions of spike count correlations for adjacent stimuli but not for superimposed/fused stimuli were also seen in V4.
source: Distinct distributions of spike count correlations based on stimulus preferences were also seen in V4 for separate objects but not when two stimuli fused to form one object.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data from V4.

claim: Multiple objects evoke different response dynamics than those evoked by single stimuli.
source: These findings suggest multiple objects evoke different response dynamics than those evoked by single stimuli, lending support to the multiplexing hypothesis and suggesting a means by which information about multiple objects can be preserved despite the apparent coarseness of sensory coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Coarse population coding has been widely explored in motor systems, where neurons show broad activity profiles and are thought to 'vote' for the movement typically associated with their peak activity.
source: Coarse population coding has been widely explored in motor systems, where neurons show broad activity profiles and are thought to 'vote' for the movement typically associated with their peak activity (e.g., Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Lee et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual motor systems only generate one movement at a time.
source: However, individual motor systems only generate one movement at a time.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about motor systems.

claim: Letters on a page are probably <0.25° apart.
source: For example, the letters on the page you are reading now are probably <0.25° apart, but foveal V1 receptive fields are approximately 0.5–2° in diameter (Dow et al., 1981; Alonso and Chen, 2009; Xing et al., 2009; Dubey and Ray, 2016; Keliris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an estimate based on typical reading conditions.

claim: Foveal V1 receptive fields are approximately 0.5–2° in diameter.
source: For example, the letters on the page you are reading now are probably <0.25° apart, but foveal V1 receptive fields are approximately 0.5–2° in diameter (Dow et al., 1981; Alonso and Chen, 2009; Xing et al., 2009; Dubey and Ray, 2016; Keliris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Receptive fields get even larger at later stages along the visual processing stream.
source: Receptive fields get even larger at later stages along the visual processing stream (e.g., Alonso and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Mammalian neurons may be responsive to nearly any location in space in the auditory system.
source: In the auditory system, mammalian neurons may be responsive to nearly any location in space (e.g., Woods et al., 2001; Groh et al., 2003; McAlpine and Grothe, 2003; Werner-Reiss and Groh, 2008; Grothe et al., 2010; Higgins et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Frequency tuning is broad at conversational sound levels in the auditory system.
source: and even frequency tuning is broad at conversational sound levels (Bulkin and Groh, 2011; Willett and Groh, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nervous system might employ a form of neural turn-taking (time division multiplexing) in which individual neurons fluctuate between responding to each of the items in or near their receptive fields across various epochs of time.
source: We have recently presented the hypothesis that the nervous system might employ a form of neural turn-taking (time division multiplexing) in which individual neurons fluctuate between responding to each of the items in or near their receptive fields across various epochs of time (Caruso et al., 2018; Mohl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors and supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: The original study on multiplexing tested one subcortical auditory area (the inferior colliculus) and one extrastriate visual cortical area (area MF of the inferotemporal [IT] face patch system).
source: Our original study tested one subcortical auditory area (the inferior colliculus) and one extrastriate visual cortical area (area MF of the inferotemporal [IT] face patch system).
evidence: This describes the scope of a previous study by the authors.

claim: V1 neurons have comparatively small receptive fields compared to more broadly tuned areas such as the inferior colliculus or inferotemporal (IT) cortex.
source: V1 allows for a strong test of these hypotheses since V1 neurons have comparatively small receptive fields and are therefore less subject to the multiple-stimulus-overlap problem than the more broadly tuned areas such as the inferior colliculus or inferotemporal (IT) cortex that were assessed in our previous report (Caruso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about V1 receptive field properties, with citation to previous work.

claim: When two gratings were superimposed, they presumably appeared as one fused object, or plaid.
source: When the two gratings were superimposed, they presumably appeared as one fused object, or plaid (Adelson and Movshon, 1982; Rodman and Albright, 1989; Heeger et al., 1996; Busse et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on plaid perception.

claim: When gratings were adjacent they appeared as two distinct objects.
source: whereas when they were adjacent they appeared as two distinct objects.
evidence: This is an inference about perception based on the stimulus configuration.

claim: Evidence for coding fluctuations was found when two gratings were present at separate locations (two objects) but not when the gratings were superimposed at the same location and appeared as one fused object.
source: We found evidence for coding fluctuations when two gratings were present at separate locations (two objects) but not when the gratings were superimposed at the same location and appeared as one fused object.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In the two-object case, the distribution of spike count correlations was markedly different from previous reports involving individual stimuli.
source: In the two-object case, the distribution of spike count correlations was markedly different from previous reports involving individual stimuli (Table 1, Cohen and Kohn, 2011), and encompassed a range spanning many negative correlations in addition to positive ones.
evidence: This is a finding from the study that compares results to previous literature.

claim: The activity of neurons in visual cortex was recorded in three experimental designs in six monkeys (N = 2 per experiment per brain area), using chronically implanted multielectrode arrays.
source: The activity of neurons in visual cortex was recorded in three experimental designs in six monkeys (N = 2 per experiment per brain area), using chronically implanted multielectrode arrays (Figure 1a, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: In the 'superimposed' dataset, the activity of neurons in V1 and V4 was recorded while monkeys passively fixated.
source: In the 'superimposed' dataset, the activity of neurons in V1 and V4 was recorded while monkeys passively fixated (for details, see Ruff et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods with citation to a previous publication.

claim: In the 'adjacent' V1 dataset, the activity of V1 neurons was recorded while monkeys fixated while performing an orientation change discrimination task.
source: In the 'adjacent' datasets, the activity of V1 and V4 neurons was recorded while monkeys either passively fixated (V4 recordings) or fixated while performing an orientation change discrimination task involving either one of these stimuli or a third stimulus presented in the ipsilateral hemifield (V1) (for details, see Ruff and Cohen, 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods with citation to a previous publication.

claim: In the 'adjacent' V4 dataset, the activity of V4 neurons was recorded while monkeys passively fixated.
source: In the 'adjacent' datasets, the activity of V1 and V4 neurons was recorded while monkeys either passively fixated (V4 recordings) or fixated while performing an orientation change discrimination task involving either one of these stimuli or a third stimulus presented in the ipsilateral hemifield (V1) (for details, see Ruff and Cohen, 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods with citation to a previous publication.

claim: In the 'superimposed' dataset, the gratings were large, spanning the receptive fields of the recorded neurons.
source: In the 'superimposed' dataset, the gratings were large, spanning the receptive fields of the recorded neurons, and were presented either individually or in combinations of two orthogonal gratings at a consistent location on every trial (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties used in the experiment.

claim: In the 'adjacent' datasets, the stimuli were smaller Gabor patches or natural images.
source: In the 'adjacent' datasets, the stimuli were smaller Gabor patches (V1, V4, Figure 1d and e) or natural images (V4, Figure 1e, stimuli from Long et al., 2018)
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties used in the experiment, with citation for natural images.

claim: For data collected during performance of the attention task (V1), analyses focused on trials in which the monkeys attended to the third stimulus and judged its orientation.
source: For data collected during performance of the attention task (V1), we focused our analyses on trials in which the monkeys attended to the third stimulus and judged its orientation, that is, attention was consistently directed away from either of the two adjacent Gabor patches that elicited responses in the neurons under study (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria for the analysis.

claim: Trials in which the monkey was required to attend to one or the other of the adjacent Gabor patches were excluded from the analyses.
source: Trials in which the monkey was required to attend to one or the other of the adjacent Gabor patches were excluded from the analyses, as were incorrectly performed trials.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria for the analysis.

claim: Fixation windows were small, ±0.5° horizontally and vertically.
source: fixation windows were small, ±0.5° horizontally and vertically, and trials with broken fixations were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes the experimental control methods.

claim: Trials with microsaccades during the stimulus presentations were excluded from further analysis.
source: Any trials with microsaccades during the stimulus presentations (defined as eye velocity exceeding 6 standard deviations above the mean velocity observed during steady fixation; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003) were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria with citation for the microsaccade definition.

claim: Only a 200 ms period after stimulus onset was analyzed.
source: Only a 200 ms period after stimulus onset was analyzed.
evidence: This describes the analysis window used in the study.

claim: Any stimulus-evoked modulation in eye position would have a latency of 150–350 ms.
source: Our reasoning is that any stimulus-evoked modulation in eye position would have a latency of 150–350 ms (Engbert and Kliegl, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There was no difference in eye position variation based on the stimulus conditions.
source: In addition, we verified that there actually was no difference in eye position variation based on the stimulus conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), so even this slim possibility was not borne out.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's control analyses.

claim: The proportion of units showing a correlation between firing rate and fixational scatter was small overall (4–9%).
source: Finally, we assessed the responses of individual units to ascertain what proportion of units showed a correlation between firing rate and fixational scatter; this proportion was small overall (4–9%) and did not co-vary with the outcomes of the main analyses of the study (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for details).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's control analyses.

claim: The dual-stimulus distributions of spike counts are over-dispersed compared to what would be expected if the spikes on dual-stimulus presentations were generated from a similar Poisson process as the single-stimulus presentations.
source: The dual-stimulus distributions of spike counts are over-dispersed compared to what would be expected if the spikes on dual-stimulus presentations were generated from a similar Poisson process as the single- stimulus presentations, and a tendency for bimodality with modes near the modes for each of the individual stimulus presentations is evident.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: 'Mixtures' were evident in a third of V1 units (33%) when two objects were presented (adjacent gratings).
source: We found that 'mixtures' were evident in a third of V1 units (33%) when two objects were presented (adjacent gratings, Figure 2c)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: 'Mixtures' were very rare (2%) in V1 when only one 'object' was present (superimposed gratings).
source: but were very rare when only one 'object' was present (superimposed gratings, Figure 2d, 2%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The incidence of 'mixtures' in V1 for the adjacent stimuli was slightly below that observed in the MF face patch in IT cortex (38%).
source: The incidence of 'mixtures' in V1 for the adjacent stimuli was slightly below that observed in the MF face patch in IT cortex (38%) and about half the rate observed in the inferior colliculus (67%; IT and IC data reanalyzed from Caruso et al., 2018 to use similar winning model criteria as shown here for this study).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous data with citation.

claim: The incidence of 'mixtures' in V1 for the adjacent stimuli was about half the rate observed in the inferior colliculus (67%).
source: The incidence of 'mixtures' in V1 for the adjacent stimuli was slightly below that observed in the MF face patch in IT cortex (38%) and about half the rate observed in the inferior colliculus (67%; IT and IC data reanalyzed from Caruso et al., 2018 to use similar winning model criteria as shown here for this study).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous data with citation.

claim: Units 1 and 2 exhibited congruent stimulus preferences: stimulus 'A,' elicited higher spike counts than stimulus 'B' for both.
source: Units 1 and 2 exhibited congruent stimulus preferences: stimulus 'A,' elicited higher spike counts (red line) than stimulus 'B' (blue line) for both.
evidence: This describes the properties of example units shown in the figures.

claim: Unit 3 had the opposite (incongruent) preference, with higher spike counts for 'B' than for 'A.'
source: Unit 3 had the opposite (incongruent) preference, with higher spike counts for 'B' than for 'A.'
evidence: This describes the properties of an example unit shown in the figures.

claim: The pairing between the units with congruent preferences yielded a positive spike count correlation value (0.56).
source: The pattern of spike count correlation on individual stimulus presentations varied depending on the stimulus tuning preferences, with the pairing between the units with congruent preferences yielding a positive value (0.56, panel d)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis of example units.

claim: The two pairings involving incongruent preferences yielded negative spike count correlations (−0.45, –0.34).
source: and the two pairings involving incongruent preferences yielding negative spike count correlations (−0.45, –0.34, panels e and f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis of example units.

claim: All the pairings that involved congruent tuning preferences yielded positive correlations, and all of these correlations are individually significant (p<0.05).
source: all the pairings that involved congruent tuning preferences yielded positive correlations, and all of these correlations are individually significant (green bars, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: All the pairings that involve incongruent tuning preferences yielded negative correlations, with 1 of 5 reaching individual significance (p<0.05).
source: In contrast, all the pairings that involve incongruent tuning preferences yielded negative correlations (brown bars); as expected, these are slightly more weakly negative than the congruent pairings are positive, but 1 of 5 reaches individual significance (darker brown, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Neural pairs in which both units responded better to the same individual stimuli tended to have positive correlations with each other (median 0.486) among 'mixtures'.
source: neural pairs in which both units responded better to the same individual stimuli tended to have positive correlations with each other ('congruent preferences,' green bars, median 0.486)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Neural pairs that had different ('incongruent') stimulus preferences tended to exhibit negative correlations (median –0.14) among 'mixtures'.
source: whereas those that had different ('incongruent') stimulus preferences tended to exhibit negative correlations (brown bars, median –0,14).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: In the adjacent-stimulus dataset, the overall broad distribution and distinction between congruent-preference and incongruent-preference subgroups holds even when not selecting for 'mixture' fluctuating patterns (median rsc 0.252, –0.052).
source: In the adjacent-stimulus dataset, the overall broad distribution and distinction between congruent-preference and incongruent-preference subgroups holds even when not selecting for 'mixture' fluctuating patterns (green bars vs. brown bars, median rsc 0.252, –0.052).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: In the superimposed-gratings dataset, there is very little difference between the congruent-preference and incongruent-preference pairs of neurons (median congruent-preference rsc = 0.159, median incongruent-preference rsc = 0.144).
source: However, this is much less true of the superimposed-gratings dataset (Figure 4f): here, there is very little difference between the congruent-preference and incongruent-preference pairs of neurons (median congruent-preference rsc = 0.159, median incongruent-preference rsc = 0.144)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: There is little difference between the spike count correlations observed on dual-gratings presentations vs. individual grating presentations for the superimposed-gratings dataset.
source: nor is there much difference between the spike count correlations observed on dual-gratings presentations vs. individual grating presentations for this dataset (orange dashed line).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: There is a distinct difference between spike count correlations observed on the dual-stimuli vs. individual-stimulus presentations in the adjacent-stimulus dataset.
source: In contrast, there is a distinct difference between spike count correlations observed on the dual-stimuli vs. individual-stimulus presentations in the adjacent-stimulus dataset (orange dashed line, Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The overall pattern of positive and negative spike count correlations evoked by two objects was not an artifact of multiunit recordings.
source: We verified that this unusual pattern of positive and negative spike count correlations evoked by two objects was not an artifact of multiunit recordings: Figure 4e shows the spike count correlation patterns observed for the subset of 24 combinations of well-isolated units recorded simultaneously in the adjacent gratings dataset.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis.

claim: All nine combinations of classifications yielded positive median spike count correlations among 'congruent' preference pairs and negative correlations among 'incongruent' preference pairs.
source: We found that all nine combinations of classifications yielded positive median spike count correlations among 'congruent' preference pairs and negative correlations among 'incongruent' preference pairs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis across different classification categories.

claim: The overall pattern of results does not rest critically on the particular details of the model comparison implemented in the study.
source: Thus, the overall pattern of results described above does not rest critically on the particular details of the model comparison we implemented here, and is present even among units that could not be formally shown to be fluctuating fully between 'A'-like and 'B'-like response distributions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the robustness of the findings.

claim: The overall positive skew in the assignment score correlations indicates a bias for the same stimulus at the same time.
source: The overall positive skew in the assignment score correlations for both the 'same' and 'different' preferring unit condition pairs (panel b) therefore indicates a bias for the same stimulus at the same time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results.

claim: The negative tail in assignment score correlations indicates the other stimulus is nevertheless also represented in a (smaller) subpopulation of neurons.
source: The negative tail indicates the other stimulus is nevertheless also represented in a (smaller) subpopulation of neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results.

claim: All stimulus presentations with microsaccades were excluded from the analyses.
source: As mentioned previously, all stimulus presentations with microsaccades were excluded from the analyses, limiting the degree to which shared dependence on eye movements could affect the correlation patterns.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Activity patterns differed considerably in the superimposed vs. adjacent stimuli cases in V4.
source: Like V1, activity patterns differed considerably in the superimposed vs. adjacent stimuli cases.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: 'Mixtures' were present in both the superimposed and adjacent stimulus conditions in V4.
source: while 'mixtures' were present in both the superimposed and adjacent stimulus conditions in V4, 'intermediates' were more prevalent in the adjacent stimulus case than in the superimposed stimulus case.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: 'Intermediates' were more prevalent in the adjacent stimulus case than in the superimposed stimulus case in V4.
source: while 'mixtures' were present in both the superimposed and adjacent stimulus conditions in V4, 'intermediates' were more prevalent in the adjacent stimulus case than in the superimposed stimulus case.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: For adjacent mixture–mixture pairs in V4, the congruent-preferring units tended to show positive spike count correlations, whereas for incongruent-preferring pairs, the distribution appeared centered around zero.
source: For adjacent mixture–mixture pairs (panel a), the congruent-preferring units again tended to show positive spike count correlations, whereas for incongruent-preferring pairs, the distribution appeared centered around zero.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: When intermediate–intermediate patterns are included in V4, the overall pattern of a difference between the congruent-preferring and incongruent-preferring distributions is preserved.
source: When intermediate–intermediate patterns are included, the overall pattern of a difference between the congruent-preferring and incongruent-preferring distributions is preserved (panel b), although now the incongruent-preference pairs are slightly positive.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: There is a distinct difference between the median spike count correlation for same-preference and different-preference pairs for the adjacent dataset in V4.
source: This pattern was still present when no selection for response pattern was applied (panel c), and is perhaps best appreciated by comparing the medians of the distributions (Figure 8f): there is a distinct difference between the median spike count correlation for same-preference and different-preference pairs for the adjacent dataset.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: Similar differences in the correlation patterns of congruent-preference vs. incongruent-preference pairs have been identified in a previous study involving responses of V4 neurons to adjacent gratings.
source: Similar differences in the correlation patterns of congruent-preference vs. incongruent-preference pairs have also been identified in a previous study involving responses of V4 neurons to adjacent gratings (Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: When the two stimuli were presented in a superimposed fashion in V4, the difference between congruent and incongruent preference pairs was no longer evident.
source: However, again like V1, when the two stimuli were presented in a superimposed fashion, this difference was no longer evident.
evidence: This is a finding from the V4 data analysis.

claim: When fluctuations do occur for superimposed/bound stimuli, they likely reflect a somewhat different underlying mechanism or purpose than when distinct stimuli are presented.
source: This was the case across the whole dataset (Figure 8e and f) as well as for mixture–mixture pairs (Figure 8d and f), suggesting that when fluctuations do occur for superimposed/bound stimuli, they likely reflect a somewhat different underlying mechanism or purpose than when distinct stimuli are presented.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Individual units show both 'A-like' and 'B-like' response patterns across trials.
source: (1) individual units show both 'A-like' and 'B-like' (red and blue) response patterns across trials – as expected since we selected 'mixture' units to include in the plot;
evidence: This is an observation from the single-session analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Pairs of units can show correlations with each other.
source: (2) pairs of units can show correlations with each other (e.g., units 1 and 2 show strongly positively correlated fluctuation patterns, and units 3–5 show positive correlations that are present but somewhat weaker).
evidence: This is an observation from the single-session analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Simultaneously recorded units do not correlate perfectly – there is considerable independence in what individual units are doing.
source: However, this figure also makes clear that simultaneously recorded units do not correlate perfectly – there is considerable independence in what individual units are doing (compare, for example, units 3–5 with units 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the single-session analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: On individual trials some units across the population are responding in an A-like fashion and others are responding in a B-like fashion.
source: The net result of this is that on individual trials some units across the population are responding in an A-like fashion and others are responding in a B-like fashion.
evidence: This is an observation from the single-session analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: At the population level, information about both stimuli is preserved on individual trials.
source: This supports our overall interpretation that, at the population level, information about both stimuli is preserved on individual trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Fluctuating activity patterns were identified in V1, evoked only by combinations of stimuli that are parsed as separate objects.
source: First, we identified fluctuating activity patterns in V1, evoked only by combinations of stimuli that are parsed as separate objects.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: Multiplexing of information may be a general characteristic of sensory signals in the brain.
source: This finding suggests not only that multiplexing of information may be a general characteristic of sensory signals in the brain, but also implicates it in the process of separating vs. grouping of stimuli into objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings.

claim: Multiplexing is implicated in the process of separating vs. grouping of stimuli into objects.
source: This finding suggests not only that multiplexing of information may be a general characteristic of sensory signals in the brain, but also implicates it in the process of separating vs. grouping of stimuli into objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings.

claim: Single objects (whether individual gratings or two superimposed gratings) yielded correlation patterns very similar to previous reports in the literature.
source: Single objects (whether individual gratings or two superimposed gratings) yielded correlation patterns very similar to previous reports in the literature (Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Ruff et al., 2016; Ruff and Cohen, 2016)
evidence: This is a finding that compares results to previous literature with citations.

claim: For single objects, the correlations did not greatly depend on whether the two units in the pair preferred the same individual stimulus or different ones.
source: and the correlations did not greatly depend on whether the two units in the pair preferred the same individual stimulus or different ones.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: When two stimuli were presented adjacent to one another, two distinct distributions emerged based on whether the two units in the pair preferred the same (congruent) individual stimulus vs. different (incongruent) individual stimuli.
source: In contrast, when two stimuli were presented adjacent to one another other, two distinct distributions emerged based on whether the two units in the pair preferred the same (congruent) individual stimulus (associated with generally positive spike count correlations) vs. different (incongruent) individual stimuli (associated with generally negative spike count correlations in V1 or simply less positive spike count correlations in V4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The pattern of positive and negative correlations exhibited between pairs of units is consistent with a population code biased toward one of the two stimuli on any given stimulus presentation, but that preserves information about the other stimulus as well.
source: The pattern of positive and negative (or less positive) correlations exhibited between pairs of such units is consistent with a population code biased toward one of the two stimuli on any given stimulus presentation, but that preserves information about the other stimulus as well.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: For most V1 'mixtures,' the observed fluctuations involved responding vs. not responding rather than fluctuating between two different levels of responding.
source: Put another way, for most of these V1 'mixtures,' the observed fluctuations involved responding vs. not responding rather than fluctuating between two different levels of responding.
evidence: This is an observation about the nature of the fluctuations in V1.

claim: The coarseness of tuning did not necessarily pose a problem for the encoding of these particular stimuli in V1.
source: Thus, the coarseness of tuning did not necessarily pose a problem for the encoding of these particular stimuli in this particular brain area, and yet fluctuations were observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The precision of V1's spatial code may not be the limiting factor for multiplexing.
source: Thus, the precision of V1's spatial code may not be the limiting factor.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings.

claim: If multiunit clusters consisted of individual neurons who were behaving differently from one another, this would be expected to work against the sensitivity of the analyses.
source: If anything, this would be expected to work against the sensitivity of the analyses, if such clusters consisted of individual neurons who were behaving differently from one another.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential confounds.

claim: The findings were broadly similar in the subset of the data that involved well-isolated single units as compared to the full dataset involving multiunit activity.
source: In fact, our findings were broadly similar in the subset of the data that involved well-isolated single units as compared to the full dataset involving multiunit activity.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis.

claim: The previous study identifying coding fluctuations in the inferior colliculus and the MF face patch of inferotemporal cortex was conducted on well-isolated single units.
source: Furthermore, our previous study identifying coding fluctuations in the inferior colliculus and the MF face patch of inferotemporal cortex was conducted on well-isolated single units (Caruso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about a previous study with citation.

claim: It is unlikely that single vs. multiunit isolation significantly impacted the findings.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that single vs. multiunit isolation significantly impacted our findings.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on control analyses and previous work.

claim: Trials with microsaccades were excluded, so such small eye movements are unlikely to have affected the findings.
source: As noted earlier, we excluded trials with microsaccades, so such small eye movements are unlikely to have affected the findings
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental controls.

claim: Fixational scatter did not vary by stimulus conditions.
source: and fixational scatter did not vary by stimulus conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis.

claim: It is unlikely that variation in fixation position contributed to the difference observed between two-object vs. fused-object response patterns or the differences between congruent-preference and incongruent-preference pairs of units.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that variation in fixation position contributed to the difference we observed between two-object vs. fused-object response patterns or the differences between congruent-preference and incongruent-preference pairs of units.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on control analyses.

claim: Similar coding fluctuations were observed in two brain areas (the IC and MF face patch) for auditory and large visual stimuli.
source: Furthermore, as noted above, we observed similar coding fluctuations in two brain areas (the IC and MF face patch) for auditory and large visual stimuli – that is, stimulus conditions that are thought to involve less sensitivity to differences in fixation position than V1 and V4 (Bremmer, 2000; Groh et al., 2001; Porter et al., 2006; Porter et al., 2007; Lehky et al., 2008; Maier and Groh, 2010; Bulkin and Groh, 2012a; Bulkin and Groh, 2012b; Merriam et al., 2013; Caruso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings with multiple citations.

claim: A previous study in V4 also reported correlation differences between congruent and incongruent preference pairs.
source: Finally, there is precedent in the literature for differences in the spike count correlation patterns of congruent vs. incongruent-preference pairs: a previous study in V4 (Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017) also reported such correlation differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The general effect size of the V4 results seems to be similar to those in the Verhoef and Maunsell study.
source: The general effect size of our V4 results seems to be similar to theirs, particularly when considering the most comparable conditions.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: The same-preference vs. different-preference correlation patterns observed in the two studies are likely to generalize across different experimental designs.
source: This suggests that the same-preference vs. different-preference correlation patterns observed in the two studies are likely to generalize across different experimental designs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison to previous work.

claim: Under the 'noise correlation' view, positive correlations have historically been seen as detrimental for encoding information at the population level.
source: Under this 'noise correlation' view, positive correlations have historically been seen as detrimental for encoding information at the population level (Shadlen and Newsome, 1994; Zohary et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Views on noise correlations have seen notable refinement and qualification since early studies.
source: Such views have also seen notable refinement and qualification since these early studies (Romo et al., 2003; Averbeck and Lee, 2004; Averbeck et al., 2006; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014; Kanitscheider et al., 2015; Kohn et al., 2016; Nogueira et al., 2020; Kafashan et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent work notes that neural variability could be a signal reflecting stimulus uncertainty.
source: including recent work noting that neural variability could be a signal reflecting stimulus uncertainty (Hénaff et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The temporal correlation hypothesis proposed that binding might be mediated through precise synchrony of spikes among neurons responding to the same object.
source: This theory focused on the need to connect the brain's representation of different attributes of a given object together, and proposed that such binding might be mediated through precise synchrony of spikes among neurons responding to the same object.
evidence: This is a description of a previous theory.

claim: Studies exploring the temporal correlation hypothesis have primarily focused on within-trial temporal synchrony of spikes on the order of milliseconds.
source: Studies exploring this hypothesis have, however, primarily focused on within-trial temporal synchrony of spikes on the order of milliseconds, whereas the noise correlation literature has focused on spike counts in the domain of hundreds of milliseconds and analysis at the level of the ensemble of trials or stimulus presentations.
evidence: This is a description of previous research approaches.

claim: The present work forges a bridge between the temporal correlation hypothesis and noise correlation literature.
source: By evaluating spike count variation at the level of stimulus presentations and comparing the results as a function of the number of stimuli/objects, the present work forges a bridge between these two areas of the literature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the contribution of the current work.

claim: Selective attention refers to the fact that perceptual awareness is not equal across all stimuli present in a sensory scene.
source: Selective attention refers to the fact that perceptual awareness is not equal across all stimuli present in a sensory scene.
evidence: This is a definition of selective attention based on established knowledge.

claim: The monkeys were performing a task in which they were in theory ignoring the stimuli whose responses were studied in the adjacent V1 dataset.
source: Indeed, the monkeys were performing just such a task in our adjacent V1 dataset, and thus were in theory ignoring the stimuli whose responses we studied here.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Top-down control of attention is imperfect even with correct task performance.
source: But even with correct task performance, top-down control of attention is imperfect.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about attention.

claim: If the fluctuating responses were due to covert shifts of attention, then the neurons should have fluctuated in more perfect harmony with one another.
source: If this were the case, then the neurons should have fluctuated in more perfect harmony with one another.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Although there is a bias in which stimulus is 'capturing' the response patterns on individual trials, there remains a substantial portion of the neural population that is responding to the other stimulus.
source: As shown quantitatively in Figure 6 and qualitatively in Figure 9, although there is a bias in which stimulus is 'capturing' the response patterns on individual trials, there remains a substantial portion of the neural population that is responding to the other stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The observed pattern of fluctuating activity is very different from a simulation of covert attention.
source: And the observed pattern of fluctuating activity is very different from a simulation of covert attention (Figure 9a vs. Figure 9d).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing data to simulations.

claim: The patterns of activity observed can in principle support preservation of information about all stimuli in the scene.
source: While further work on this question is needed, we think it is worth noting that the patterns of activity that we observed can in principle support preservation of information about all stimuli in the scene.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Processes involved in selective attention might contribute to the creation of biases within this representation or could act at later stages on the information preserved within these representations to enhance awareness of one or more of the represented stimuli.
source: Processes involved in selective attention might contribute to the creation of biases within this representation or could act at later stages on the information preserved within these representations to enhance awareness of one or more of the represented stimuli.
evidence: This is speculation about how attention might interact with the observed phenomena.

claim: Trial-averaged neural responses to attended and unattended stimuli can often be modeled as a weighted combination of the responses to those stimuli when presented alone.
source: Trial-averaged neural responses to attended and unattended stimuli can often be modeled as a weighted combination of the responses to those stimuli when presented alone (Boynton, 2009; Lee and Maunsell, 2009; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Ni et al., 2012; Ni and Maunsell, 2017; Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017; Ni and Maunsell, 2019; Lee and Maunsell, 2009; Ni et al., 2012; Ni and Maunsell, 2017; Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017; Ni and Maunsell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Such averaging responses are seen not only in attention paradigms but in other contexts as well and are generally referred to as normalization.
source: Such averaging responses are seen not only in attention paradigms but in other contexts as well (e.g., see also Xiao et al., 2014; Xiao and Huang, 2015) and are generally referred to as normalization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Such apparently averaging responses might actually indicate fluctuations occurring on either the stimulus presentation or sub-stimulus presentation timescales, and not a true stable average.
source: Trial-wise spike count distribution models such as those used here and/or faster subtrial analyses such as those we have introduced in previous work (Caruso et al., 2018; Glynn et al., 2021) might indicate that such apparently averaging responses actually indicate fluctuations occurring on either the stimulus presentation or sub-stimulus presentation timescales, and not a true stable average (e.g., Figure 9a vs. Figure 9e).
evidence: This is speculation about reinterpretation of previous findings, with citations to methods.

claim: Several important recent studies have begun to explore how recurrent circuit mechanisms might implement dynamic fluctuations in neural activity.
source: For example, several important recent studies have begun to explore how recurrent circuit mechanisms might implement dynamic fluctuations in neural activity (Heeger and Mackey, 2019; Heeger and Zemlianova, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Shifts in the balanced excitation and inhibition that is thought to underlie normalized average responses when two stimuli are presented might contribute to sizeable positive or negative spike count correlations.
source: and have postulated that shifts in the balanced excitation and inhibition that is thought to underlie normalized average responses when two stimuli are presented might contribute to sizeable positive or negative spike count correlations (Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent work by Coen-Cagli and colleagues proposes a method of assessing normalization strength on individual trials and demonstrated a connection between the neural responses that are well-described under a normalization model and the level of variability of firing that they show.
source: Finally, recent work by Coen-Cagli and colleagues proposes a method of assessing normalization strength on individual trials and demonstrated a connection between the neural responses that are well-described under a normalization model and the level of variability of firing that they show (Coen-Cagli and Solomon, 2019; Weiss et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The likelihood of detecting a brief near-threshold visual stimulus varies with the phase of the brain wave oscillations at the time the stimulus is presented.
source: The likelihood of detecting a brief near-threshold visual stimulus varies with the phase of the brain wave oscillations at the time the stimulus is presented (Busch et al., 2009; Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Vanrullen et al., 2011; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Fiebelkorn et al., 2018; Helfrich et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019; see also Engel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: This might reflect a perceptual consequence of a brain mechanism in which neurons are slightly biased toward representing some stimuli in the visual scene over others in a naturally occurring oscillatory fashion.
source: This might reflect a perceptual consequence of a brain mechanism in which neurons are slightly biased toward representing some stimuli in the visual scene over others in a naturally occurring oscillatory fashion.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying previous findings.

claim: In a previous study, the LFP signal prior to stimulus onset was predictive of whether neurons would 'pick' A vs. B on a given trial.
source: In our previous study (Caruso et al., 2018), we found that the LFP signal prior to stimulus onset was predictive of whether neurons would 'pick' A vs. B on a given trial.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: When the number of objects gets too great, it is unlikely that neurons can fluctuate between all of them, and this is likely to have consequences for perception.
source: When the number of objects gets too great, it is unlikely that neurons can fluctuate between all of them, and this is likely to have consequences for perception, perhaps accounting for well-known limits on the number of objects we can perceive, attend to, and remember (e.g., Miller, 1956; Whitney and Levi, 2011; Henry and Kohn, 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about the limits of the mechanism, with citations to previous work on perceptual limits.

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University (Protocol #: 20067560 PHS Assurance Number: D16-00118).
source: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University (Protocol #: 20067560 PHS Assurance Number: D16-00118).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Each of the datasets consisted of multielectrode recordings from two adult male rhesus monkeys for each brain area.
source: Each of the datasets consisted of multielectrode recordings from two adult male rhesus monkeys for each brain area (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Recordings were made using chronically implanted a 10 × 10 microelectrode arrays in V1 and 6 × 8 arrays in V4.
source: Recordings were made using chronically implanted a 10 × 10 microelectrode arrays (Blackrock Microsystems) in V1 and 6 × 8 arrays in V4 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the recording methods.

claim: The electrode shafts were 1 mm long, and the minimum distance between the nearest electrodes was 400 μm.
source: The electrode shafts were 1 mm long, and the minimum distance between the nearest electrodes was 400 μm.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the recording equipment.

claim: In most sessions, each stimulus lasted for 200 ms.
source: In most sessions, each stimulus lasted for 200 ms; a few sessions with 1000 ms stimuli were also included but only the first 200 ms were analyzed
evidence: This describes the stimulus timing parameters.

claim: Spikes were counted in a 200 ms window after stimulus onset for all the analyses in this study.
source: that is, spikes were counted in a 200 ms window after stimulus onset for all the analyses in this study.
evidence: This describes the analysis window.

claim: This spike counting window was offset by the typical response latency for the region under study, that is, 30–230 ms for V1 and 50–250 ms for V4.
source: This spike counting window was offset by the typical response latency for the region under study, that is, 30–230 ms for V1 and 50–250 ms for V4.
evidence: This describes the analysis parameters adjusted for response latency.

claim: The animals performed a motion direction change detection task in which they were cued in blocks of trials to attend to small drifting Gabor patches in various locations and respond when the orientation of the attended location changed.
source: The animals performed a motion direction change detection task in which they were cued in blocks of trials to attend to small drifting Gabor patches (~1o) in various locations and respond when the orientation of the attended location changed.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task.

claim: The patches had the same orientation but drifted in opposite directions and were flashed on for 200 ms and off for 200–400 ms.
source: The patches had the same orientation but drifted in opposite directions and were flashed on for 200 ms and off for 200–400 ms.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: Only correctly performed trials with no microsaccades during stimulus presentations were included for analysis.
source: Again, only correctly performed trials with no microsaccades during stimulus presentations were included for analysis.
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: The adjacent stimulus dataset for V4 involved two types of stimuli, small drifting Gabor patches or natural images of animals or common objects.
source: The adjacent stimulus dataset for V4 involved two types of stimuli, small drifting Gabor patches as above or natural images of animals or common objects, from Long et al., 2018.
evidence: This describes the stimulus types with citation for natural images.

claim: The monkeys performed a fixation task in the V4 adjacent stimulus dataset.
source: The monkeys performed a fixation task.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task.

claim: A Bayesian procedure was deployed for modeling the distribution of spike counts in response to combined stimuli.
source: Briefly, we deployed a Bayesian procedure for modeling the distribution of spike counts in response to combined stimuli.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: The spike counts corresponding to condition A and condition B are both assumed to be Poisson-distributed with the rate parameters λA and λB, respectively.
source: Assuming that the spike counts corresponding to condition A and condition B are both Poisson-distributed with the rate parameters λA and λB, respectively (and excluding exceptions, see below)
evidence: This describes the statistical assumptions of the analysis.

claim: Only the triplets satisfying two exclusion criteria are used: (1) the single-stimulus distributions follow Poisson distributions, and (2) the single-stimulus rate parameters λA and λB are substantially separated.
source: Only the triplets satisfying two exclusion criteria are used: (1) the single-stimulus distributions follow Poisson distributions, and (2) the single-stimulus rate parameters λA and λB are substantially separated.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: The first criterion was tested using Monte Carlo p-value calculation for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test (p>0.10).
source: The first criterion was tested using Monte Carlo p-value calculation for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test (p>0.10)
evidence: This describes the statistical test used.

claim: The second criterion was tested by whether the intrinsic Bayes factor of the model λA ≠ λB is more than three times higher than that of the model λA = λB.
source: and the second criterion was tested by whether the intrinsic Bayes factor of the model λA ≠ λB is more than three times higher than that of the model λA = λB.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used.

claim: Model identification accuracy in simulations is high for trial counts as low as 5 'AB' trials, and plateaus near ceiling around 'AB' trial counts of about 10 trials and above.
source: Depending on the separation between λA and λB, we previously found that model identification accuracy in simulations is high for trial counts as low as 5 'AB' trials, and plateaus near ceiling around 'AB' trial counts of about 10 trials and above – that is, below the mean trial counts available here for all datasets (see Figure 4 of Mohl et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Spike count correlations were calculated between pairs of units recorded at the same time in the same experiment.
source: We calculated spike count correlations between pairs of units recorded at the same time in the same experiment.
evidence: This describes the analysis method.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient was calculated on the spike counts for each presentation of each relevant stimulus combination.
source: The Pearson correlation coefficient was calculated on the spike counts for each presentation of each relevant stimulus combination.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: Stimulus presentations in which one or both units in the pair exhibited an 'outlier' response, that is, more than 3 standard deviations from the mean, were excluded from the analysis.
source: Stimulus presentations in which one or both units in the pair exhibited an 'outlier' response, that is, more than 3 standard deviations from the mean, were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Preference of a unit for a particular stimulus was determined by higher spike counts.
source: Preference of a unit for a particular stimulus was determined by higher spike counts.
evidence: This describes the method for determining stimulus preference.

claim: Unit pairs that both exhibited more spikes in response to stimulus A than to B, or both exhibited more spikes in response to stimulus B than to A, were defined as 'congruent preference.'
source: Unit pairs that both exhibited more spikes in response to stimulus A than to B, or both exhibited more spikes in response to stimulus B than to A, were defined as 'congruent preference.'
evidence: This describes the definition of congruent preference.

claim: Unit pairs in which one responded with more spikes to A and the other with more spikes to B were defined as 'incongruent preference'.
source: Unit pairs in which one responded with more spikes to A and the other with more spikes to B were defined as 'incongruent preference'.
evidence: This describes the definition of incongruent preference.

claim: The medians of the 'congruent preference' vs. 'incongruent preference' distributions of spike count correlations were statistically compared using Monte Carlo methods in which the same/different preference assignments were randomly shuffled and the medians recalculated 10,000 times.
source: The medians of the 'congruent preference' vs. 'incongruent preference' distributions of spike count correlations were statistically compared using Monte Carlo methods in which the same/different preference assignments were randomly shuffled and the medians recalculated 10,000 times.
evidence: This describes the statistical comparison method.
